title: Trapping Rain Water
statement:
You get an elevation map: heights[i] is the height of a bar of width 1 at position i. Rain falls and water settles between the bars. Water can spill off both ends of the map.

Write def solution(heights) that returns the total units of water trapped, as an int. One unit is one 1 x 1 cell.

The water above bar i is min(tallest bar on its left, tallest bar on its right) - heights[i], counting bar i itself on both sides, so it is never negative.

examples.why: The classic picture. Pools of 1 (index 2), 1 + 2 + 1 (indexes 4 to 6) and 1 (index 9).
The left wall is 4 and the right wall is 5, so the water line is 4: 2 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 9.
One gap of depth 3 between two walls of height 3.

constraints: hidden tests include a large input: an O(N^2) scan will time out

think.q: What decides how much water sits on top of one bar?
think.a: The lower of the two walls around it. Bar i holds min(maxLeft, maxRight) - heights[i], where the maxes include bar i. The answer is that number summed over all bars.
maxLeft is 4 4 4 4 4 5, maxRight is 5 5 5 5 5 5. The min is 4 for the first five bars. Water: 0 2 4 1 2 0 = 9.

think.q: What is the first correct thing you could write?
think.a: For each bar, scan left for the max and scan right for the max. That is O(N) work per bar, O(N^2) total: 10^10 steps for 100,000 bars, far too slow for a HackerRank hidden test.

"left max" and "right max" for every index → either prefix maxima (two arrays, O(N) space) or two pointers (O(1) space). The two-pointer insight: if heights[left] < heights[right], the bar at right is taller than every bar you have passed on the left, so it is taller than left_max. The water line at left is therefore left_max. Settle that bar and move on.

1. Set left = 0, right = n - 1, both maxes to 0, water = 0.
  2. While left < right: if heights[left] < heights[right], update left_max, add left_max - heights[left], step left right.
  3. Otherwise do the mirror image on the right side.
  4. Return water.

Empty list and one bar (no water, and no index errors). Strictly rising or falling bars (0). A flat floor of zeros. Equal walls, like [5, 0, 0, 5], where the tie branch must still work. A tall bar in the middle, which splits the map into two pools with different water lines. A taller left wall, so the right pointer does all the work.

hints: Write the formula first: water at i = min(max(heights[:i+1]), max(heights[i:])) - heights[i]. That is your brute force. Now make the two maxes cheap.
You can precompute left_max[i] in one pass left to right and right_max[i] in one pass right to left. That is O(N) time and O(N) space, which already passes.

For O(1) space, use two pointers. Whichever end has the lower bar is limited by its own running max, because the other side is at least that tall. Settle that bar, add its water, and move that pointer inward.
solution:
def solution(heights):
    # Water on bar i = min(max to its left, max to its right) - heights[i].
    # Two pointers: the side with the lower bar is capped by its own running max,
    # because the other side already has a wall at least that tall.
    left, right = 0, len(heights) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0
    water = 0
    while left < right:
        if heights[left] < heights[right]:
            left_max = max(left_max, heights[left])
            water += left_max - heights[left]
            left += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, heights[right])
            water += right_max - heights[right]
            right -= 1
    return water
brute:
def solution(heights):
    # O(N^2): for every bar, scan for the tallest bar on each side (including itself)
    water = 0
    for i in range(len(heights)):
        left_max = max(heights[:i + 1])
        right_max = max(heights[i:])
        water += min(left_max, right_max) - heights[i]
    return water
explain:
Trace [4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5]. Pointers start at both ends.

  • 4 < 5: settle the left. left_max = 4, water += 0. Move left to index 1.
  • 2 < 5: water += 4 - 2 = 2. Index 2: 0 < 5, water += 4. Index 3: 3 < 5, water += 1. Index 4: 2 < 5, water += 2.
  • Now left == right, stop. Total 2 + 4 + 1 + 2 = 9.

Why is it safe to use only left_max? The right pointer only moves past a bar when some left bar is at least as tall. So while you are moving the left pointer, the bar at right is taller than every bar you have passed on the left, including the one that set left_max. The right side can hold the water up to left_max, and the left side cannot hold more. In the OA, say this argument out loud or in a comment: it is the part graders and interviewers look for.

If you blank on the two-pointer proof under time pressure, write the two prefix-max arrays. It is also O(N) and passes the hidden tests.

extensions: Return the water above each bar as a list instead of the total. The prefix-max version gives this almost for free.
Solve it with a monotonic stack that fills water layer by layer. Be ready to say why it is also O(N).
Bars now have different widths, widths[i]. Multiply each bar's water depth by its width.
The 2D version (LeetCode 407): a height grid. Use a min-heap seeded with the border cells and flood inward.
Heights arrive one by one as a stream and you must report the total so far. Which parts of the answer can change when a new tall bar arrives?
